name: Bonaire, Saba and Sint Eustatius
rule: The official current BES Invoeringswet, article 18.2.4a(c)–(d), limits plants to living plants/parts and plant products to unprocessed products or products subjected only to simple processing. Article 18.2.4b authorises import conditions within that scope; it does not itself impose a certificate on every plant-derived food. The described steamed, repeatedly rolled/pressed, hot-air dried sencha is a finished manufactured food, with ISPM32 Category 1 tea providing technical corroboration. The better general-category inference places it beyond simple processing and therefore outside that plant-product control class. This applies the BES statute itself, which covers Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, rather than importing European Netherlands rules or extending Bonaire’s Venezuela-only notice. The statutory used-packaging category does not create a duty for clean new factory and postal packaging. No contrary applicable tea or broad manufactured-food condition was recovered in the bounded island/national rule check.
personalMailApplicability: This conclusion follows commodity scope in the applicable local law, not a baggage, gift or noncommercial-seller exception. It applies to the stated private direct postal purchase and clean new packaging.
researchAttempts: Read Bonaire’s dried-herb import notice; it specifically concerns Venezuela. Searched Japanese tea rules and Saba/Sint Eustatius coverage without finding a shared personal-post exemption.

2026-09-30: Reviewed BES Invoeringswet articles 18.2.4a–b: plant products are unprocessed or simply processed and the Minister/director may impose import conditions. Native Dutch searches did not produce a current sencha classification or implementing Japan-tea conditions across all three islands. Neither the Venezuela-only Bonaire reopening nor tax treatment resolves this shared shipping code.

2026-09-30: Warenwet BES article 2(1) excludes manufacture within the same private household, not purchased-food import generally. Article3(1)(j)–(k) empowers implementing import/export and registration rules; it does not itself impose a universal imported-food origin certificate. Article3(4) allows rules for particular BES islands. Read current official indexed 2023 text and FAOLEX 2023 full-text copy. No material new common three-island personal postal food exemption or mandatory certificate found. Existing manufactured-tea/island-specific implementing-rule gap remains.

2026-09-30 fresh official online recovery: Recovered the official legislative explanatory memorandum for BES Invoeringswet. It explicitly declines to extend the European Netherlands plant-health system to the islands, instead using the limited BES powers under articles 18.2.4a–e. This independently confirms why European/Dutch tea exemptions cannot be transferred to BQ. It does not establish the current Japanese-tea conditions common to Bonaire, Saba and Sint Eustatius. 30 September renewed general-definition review, superseding the earlier demand for a local tea-specific classification: The official current BES Invoeringswet, article 18.2.4a(c)–(d), limits plants to living plants/parts and plant products to unprocessed products or products subjected only to simple processing. Article 18.2.4b authorises import conditions within that scope; it does not itself impose a certificate on every plant-derived food. The described steamed, repeatedly rolled/pressed, hot-air dried sencha is a finished manufactured food, with ISPM32 Category 1 tea providing technical corroboration. The better general-category inference places it beyond simple processing and therefore outside that plant-product control class. This applies the BES statute itself, which covers Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, rather than importing European Netherlands rules or extending Bonaire’s Venezuela-only notice. The statutory used-packaging category does not create a duty for clean new factory and postal packaging. No contrary applicable tea or broad manufactured-food condition was recovered in the bounded island/national rule check. The actual product is pure Camellia sinensis sencha manufactured by steaming to arrest enzyme activity, repeated rolling/pressing with hot air, and drying, then supplied sealed for infusion. MAFF describes this manufacture. ISPM32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify manufactured tea as Category 1, supporting the factual conclusion that this differs from merely dried raw botanical material. The international standard is used as technical evidence when applying the local definition, not as an automatically binding local exemption. Ordinary inspection, food safety and pest freedom remain conditions; this is not a route for raw/sun-dried leaves, seeds, blends or contaminated goods.

definitionReview: Proposal for independent root review; not yet merged. See caribbean-finished-tea-definition-review/review-notes.json.
foodImportReview: The prior Warenwet BES review found regulation-making powers rather than a universal origin-certificate duty for private sealed food. This proposal changes the plant-category assessment only; it does not extend any European food-import concession or claim a personal household manufacture exception for this paid purchase.
